Contrasts, joint tests and slopes

Source: vignettes/contrasts.Rmd
contrasts.Rmd

predictmeans() gives the means of a model term and all their pairwise comparisons. This vignette shows what to use when the questions are different: comparisons with a control, trends, tests of several contrasts at once, slopes of a covariate, and other adjustments for multiple testing. The results match emmeans, pbkrtest and lmerTest (Kenward–Roger and Satterthwaite) and SAS LSMEANS, SLICE and ESTIMATE statements.

We use the oats split plot again: three varieties on whole plots within six blocks, four nitrogen levels on subplots.

library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$N <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ N * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)

Adjusting for multiple comparisons

adj sets how the p-values of the pairwise comparisons are adjusted. Besides the p.adjust() methods ("holm", "BH", "bonferroni", …) and "tukey", there are "sidak", "scheffe" and "mvt". "mvt" is the single-step multivariate t adjustment: it uses the correlations among the comparisons, so it is exact for any family of contrasts. It is what SAS ADJUST=SIMULATE estimates by simulation; here it is computed by package mvtnorm.

p <- sapply(c("none", "tukey", "mvt", "sidak", "scheffe", "holm"), function(a)
  predictmeans(fm, "N", adj = a, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)$pairs$p.adj)
pm <- predictmeans(fm, "N", plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
data.frame(pair = paste(pm$pairs$level1, "-", pm$pairs$level2), signif(p, 3))
#>        pair     none    tukey      mvt    sidak  scheffe     holm
#> 1   0 - 0.2 6.66e-05 3.76e-04 3.66e-04 3.99e-04 1.01e-03 2.00e-04
#> 2   0 - 0.4 5.65e-10 3.36e-09 1.32e-09 3.39e-09 1.55e-08 2.82e-09
#> 3 0.2 - 0.4 1.21e-03 6.39e-03 6.38e-03 7.21e-03 1.34e-02 2.41e-03
#> 4   0 - 0.6 6.70e-13 4.26e-12 1.73e-13 4.02e-12 2.15e-11 4.02e-12
#> 5 0.2 - 0.6 1.58e-06 9.24e-06 5.43e-06 9.50e-06 3.12e-05 6.33e-06
#> 6 0.4 - 0.6 4.46e-02 1.80e-01 1.80e-01 2.39e-01 2.48e-01 4.46e-02

For all pairs of means Tukey and "mvt" agree, up to the accuracy of the mvtnorm computation (about 1e-4, which shows only for very small p-values); "mvt" also covers other families, as below. Scheffé protects every possible contrast and is the most conservative.

Families of contrasts

contrast_family() builds standard sets of contrasts among the means of a term, with the same coefficients and names as emmeans: "pairwise", "revpairwise", "trt.vs.ctrl", "consec", "poly", "eff" and "del.eff". The result goes to contrastmeans().

Each nitrogen level against no nitrogen (Dunnett’s comparisons), with the exact Dunnett adjustment:

K <- Kmatrix(fm, "N")
dunnett <- contrast_family(K, "trt.vs.ctrl")
dunnett
#>          0 0.2 0.4 0.6
#> 0.2 - 0 -1   1   0   0
#> 0.4 - 0 -1   0   1   0
#> 0.6 - 0 -1   0   0   1
contrastmeans(fm, "N", ctrmatrix = dunnett, adj = "mvt")[[1]]
#>         Estimate Std. Error t value df Pr(>|t|)
#> 0.2 - 0  19.5000     4.4358  4.3961 45    2e-04
#> 0.4 - 0  34.8333     4.4358  7.8529 45    0e+00
#> 0.6 - 0  44.0000     4.4358  9.9194 45    0e+00
#> attr(,"Note")
#> [1] "The p-value is adjusted by 'mvt' method, if p-value = 0 means p-value < 0.0001."

Linear and quadratic trends in nitrogen within each variety (by), with integer orthogonal polynomial coefficients (the nitrogen levels are equally spaced):

K2 <- Kmatrix(fm, "N:Variety")
trends <- contrast_family(K2, "poly", by = "Variety", max.degree = 2)
contrastmeans(fm, "N:Variety", ctrmatrix = trends)[[1]]
#>                        Estimate Std. Error t value df Pr(>|t|)
#> Golden Rain: linear    150.6667    24.2956  6.2014 45   0.0000
#> Golden Rain: quadratic  -8.3333    10.8653 -0.7670 45   0.4471
#> Marvellous: linear     129.1667    24.2956  5.3165 45   0.0000
#> Marvellous: quadratic  -12.1667    10.8653 -1.1198 45   0.2688
#> Victory: linear        162.1667    24.2956  6.6747 45   0.0000
#> Victory: quadratic     -10.5000    10.8653 -0.9664 45   0.3390
#> attr(,"Note")
#> [1] "The p-value is adjusted by 'none' method, if p-value = 0 means p-value < 0.0001."

specify_contrast() (see the getting-started vignette) writes any other contrast by the names of the means.

Joint tests and slices

pm_joint() tests several contrasts at once with an F test. With by, it compares the means of the term within each level of the by factor, which is SAS LSMEANS N*Variety / SLICE=Variety:

pm_joint(fm, "N:Variety", by = "Variety")
#>       Variety df1 df2   F.ratio      p.value
#> 1 Golden Rain   3  45 13.022765 2.969047e-06
#> 2  Marvellous   3  45  9.952878 3.769265e-05
#> 3     Victory   3  45 15.315709 5.256928e-07
pm_joint(fm, "N:Variety", by = "N")
#>     N df1      df2   F.ratio   p.value
#> 1   0   2 30.23076 1.2245400 0.3080589
#> 2 0.2   2 30.23076 1.8814476 0.1697812
#> 3 0.4   2 30.23076 0.2156336 0.8072596
#> 4 0.6   2 30.23076 0.4010511 0.6731259

The first table asks whether nitrogen matters within each variety, the second whether the varieties differ at each nitrogen level. With ctrmatrix, the rows of any contrast matrix are tested together, e.g. the departure from a straight line (quadratic and cubic terms):

curv <- contrast_family(K, "poly")[c("quadratic", "cubic"), ]
pm_joint(fm, "N", ctrmatrix = curv)
#>   df1 df2  F.ratio   p.value
#> 1   2  45 1.366873 0.2652819

For REML lmer fits the test is the Kenward–Roger F test (as pbkrtest::KRmodcomp()); df_method = "Satterthwaite" gives lmerTest’s test, and "containment" the SAS containment df.

Slopes of a covariate

When nitrogen is used as a number, the question is how fast yield rises with it in each variety. pm_slopes() gives the slopes with standard errors, df, confidence limits and tests, and compares them (as emmeans::emtrends()):

fm2 <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)
pm_slopes(fm2, "nitro", "Variety", adj = "tukey")
#> Slopes of 'nitro' at 0.3 
#> 
#>      Variety slope std.error df conf.low conf.high statistic   p.value
#>  Golden Rain 75.33     11.86 51    51.53     99.14     6.353 5.726e-08
#>   Marvellous 64.58     11.86 51    40.78     88.39     5.446 1.490e-06
#>      Victory 81.08     11.86 51    57.28    104.89     6.838 9.828e-09
#> 
#> Pairwise differences of slopes (p.adj: tukey)
#> 
#>       level1     level2 estimate std.error df statistic p.value  p.adj
#>  Golden Rain Marvellous    10.75     16.77 51    0.6410  0.5244 0.7982
#>  Golden Rain    Victory    -5.75     16.77 51   -0.3429  0.7331 0.9373
#>   Marvellous    Victory   -16.50     16.77 51   -0.9839  0.3298 0.5903

The slopes are in yield per unit of nitrogen. With poly() or spline terms the slope changes along the covariate; at sets where it is taken (the default is the covariate’s mean).

Any contrast from coef() and vcov()

coef() and vcov() give the means of a predictmeans() result and their covariance matrix (Kenward–Roger adjusted for REML lmer fits), named by the levels. Any contrast can be computed from them:

pmv <- predictmeans(fm, "N:Variety", plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
b <- coef(pmv)
L <- (names(b) == "0.6:Victory") - (names(b) == "0.6:Golden Rain")
c(estimate = sum(L * b), SE = sqrt(drop(L %*% vcov(pmv) %*% L)))
#>  estimate        SE 
#> -6.333333  9.715020

They also let other packages test contrasts of the means. marginaleffects needs the class listed first; b1, b2, … are the means in the order of coef():

options(marginaleffects_model_classes = "predictmeans")
i <- match(c("0.6:Victory", "0.6:Golden Rain"), names(b))
marginaleffects::hypotheses(pmv, hypothesis = sprintf("b%d - b%d = 0", i[1], i[2]))
#> 
#>  Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>   b12-b10=0    -6.33       9.72 -0.652    0.514 1.0 -25.4   12.7

marginaleffects uses normal-based tests; the standard error is the same as above.
